dictamen … — “First the command of reason, then of the will, then of desire.”
Like Hindemith — Schmitt owned and knew Hindemith’s Unterweisung im Tonsatz.
On 24 November 1947 he wrote to Wilhelm Fraenger:

“I am reading Hindemith’s wonderful theory of composition—published by Schott in Mainz in 1940—and I cannot stop thinking about what you say on p. 80 of your Bosch book. Could you not somehow bring it to Hindemith’s attention? It would have to thrill him.”
Wilhelm Fraenger, correspondence with Hans Arp, Carl Schmitt and Franz Roh, in Sinn und Form 57, 2005, p. 323.

The reference is to Fraenger’s interpretation of the right-hand inner panel of The Garden of Earthly Delights, which he calls the “Musical Hell,” in W. Fraenger, Das Tausendjährige Reich, Coburg 1947.

Radbruch and Schwinge — The jurists Gustav Radbruch (1878–1949), whom Schmitt had already criticized in his doctoral dissertation but with whom he was still on friendly terms in 1930—see Tb 1930–34, p. 166—and Erich Schwinge (1903–1994), who in 1930 called Schmitt a “Sphinx among modern constitutional lawyers,” both took a critical view of Schmitt after 1945.
See also below, notes to pp. 103 and 125.
Brother Straubinger — A figure from a nineteenth-century student drinking song who represents a rogue or tramp. Carl Schmitt uses the name for Hitler.

in the manner of the German-Slovak exchange — After the annexation of the Sudetenland and the resulting weakening of the Czechoslovak Republic, Slovakia declared itself autonomous within Czechoslovakia in October 1938.
Hitler wanted an independent Slovak state and brought this about in March 1939 by placing massive pressure on Slovak prime minister Jozef Tiso.
See also below, note to p. 292.
“only the pilgrim will bless it” — Final line of Annette von Droste-Hülshoff’s poem “Mein Beruf.”
Ginés de Sepúlveda — Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda (1490–1573), Spanish theologian and historian to Charles V and Philip II.

Against Bartolomé de Las Casas, he argued that the Indigenous peoples of the Americas were savages and barbarians and therefore, on the basis of Aristotle, lacked legal rights, so that their lands could be treated as open to free seizure.
See G. de Sepúlveda, Democrates alter, sive Dialogus de justis belli causis adversus Indios, ed. Menéndez Pelayo, Boletín de la Real Academia de la Historia, XXI, Madrid 1892.
ἀναγκαζόμενος — See above, note to p. 18.
hic et nunc — “Here and now.” One of Schmitt’s personal mottos.

Vitoria, Francisco de — c. 1483–1546, Spanish theologian, Dominican friar, and scholar of international law. Founder of the School of Salamanca and a critic of Spanish practices of conquest in Latin America.
See C. Schmitt, “Francisco de Vitoria und die Geschichte seines Ruhmes,” in Die neue Ordnung 3, 1949, pp. 289–313.
my meeting with Don Theodore Andres — See above, p. 18, “Marcos.”
Schmitt met him during his lecture tour in Spain in June 1943. See Christian Tilitzki, “Die Vortragsreisen Carl Schmitts während des Zweiten Weltkriegs,” in Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 235.
unintended and merely faithful — Paraphrase of Konrad Weiß. See C. Schmitt, “Was habe ich getan?” in Schmittiana V, 1996, p. 19.
naked as at birth — Quotation from Theodor Däubler’s poem “Perseus,” in T. Däubler, Dichtungen und Schriften, ed. Friedhelm Kemp, Munich 1956, p. 250:
“Now you stand naked, naked as at birth, in desolate expanses.”
being is all I possess — Allusion to the poem “Manchmal, wenn man sich vergißt” by Konrad Weiß, dedicated to Carl Schmitt.
Coeli tonitralia templa lacessens … — “Challenging the temples and thunder of heaven, he tore the lightning bolt from Zeus and the arrows from Phoebus.”
A modified version of this quotation appeared on Houdon’s bust of Benjamin Franklin, inventor of the lightning rod.
On the Anti-Lucretius, see Rainer Specht, “Über Polignacs Antilucretius,” in Epirrhosis. Festgabe für Carl Schmitt, ed. H. Barion / E.-W. Böckenförde / W. Weber, 2nd ed., Berlin 2002, pp. 697–707.
Schmitt gave his copy of Polignac to Specht and referred to this essay in the dedication.

Nec iuvat innumeros alibi confingere mundos … — “There is no use inventing countless other worlds in which masses of every conceivable thing whirl about, while giving almost nothing to our own realm … The atoms must be given a measure, a boundary, and a restraint.”
occasio proxima — “A proximate occasion,” a term from Catholic moral theology.
Michelet’s book — Jules Michelet, Pologne et Russie. Légende de Kosciusko, Paris 1852.
Schmitt is referring to the following passage on pp. 131–132:

“We must therefore, provisionally and simply, regard Russia as a whole as a force—a barbaric force, a world without law, a world hostile to Law, making no progress in that direction but on the contrary moving backward and returning to ancient barbarism; a world that accepts modern civilization only in order to dissolve the Western world and kill Law itself.
The world of Law has its frontier where it had it in the Middle Ages: on the Vistula and the Danube.”
Kütemeyer’s afterword — Søren Kierkegaard, Der Begriff der Ironie mit ständiger Rücksicht auf Sokrates, translated by Wilhelm Kütemeyer, Munich 1929.
Ne judicate, ne iudicemini … — Vulgate, Matthew 7:1:
“Judge not, that you be not judged.”
cache ta vie et répands ton esprit — “Hide your life and spread your spirit.”
From Victor Hugo’s poem “À un poète.”
Annette writes to Sprickmann — Schmitt quotes from A. von Droste-Hülshoff, Die Briefe der Dichterin Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, ed. and annotated by Hermann Cardauns, Münster 1909.
“Were you meant to have been a deception, you blessed silver-blue day?” — Correctly:
“Were you meant to have been in vain, You blessed silver-blue day?”
See also BW Mohler, p. 104; BW EJ, p. 146.
Deus sive Natura — “God, or rather Nature.”
Schmitt repeatedly felt provoked by this equation in Spinoza. His reaction to it can already be found in his 1919 lectures on Hobbes.
Africana — Theodor Däubler, L’Africana, novel, Berlin-Grunewald 1928.
Kluxen — Franz Kluxen (1887–1968), businessman, art collector, fellow student and friend of Schmitt from Strasbourg.
Schmitt says below, p. 114, that Kluxen “initiated me into the cult of genius that shaped the spiritual world of nineteenth-century Germany …”
“Whoever ruined his longing for the sake of some worldly good” — From the poem “Am ersten Sonntag im Advent” by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff.
Here the reference is to the Greek New Testament, 1 Corinthians 4:13. In Luther’s translation:
“We have become like the scum of humanity, everyone’s refuse, to this very day.”
in the “Three Types” (p. 17) — C. Schmitt, On the Three Types of Juristic Thought, 3rd ed., Berlin 2006, pp. 14–15.
mysterium iniquitatis — The “mystery of evil” held back by the Katéchon (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7). See below, note to p. 47.
To deceive someone into the truth — This refers to the following passage in Kierkegaard:

“Do not let the word ‘deception’ deceive you. A person can be deceived about what is true; but, to recall old Socrates, a person can also be deceived into the truth. In fact, this is really the only way to bring someone who is trapped in an illusion into the truth: by deceiving him.”
Søren Kierkegaard, Gesammelte Werke, section 33: Die Schriften über sich selbst, Düsseldorf/Cologne 1964, p. 48.
May a person allow himself to be killed for the truth? — See below, note to p. 208.
Bernanos in Geneva — In September 1946 Georges Bernanos gave an impassioned speech in Geneva in which he said: “European civilization is collapsing, and nothing will replace it.”
Ecce ancilla — Dixit autem Maria ecce ancilla Domini: “And Mary said: Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord.” Vulgate, Luke 1:38.
μάκρος ἄνθρωπος — “Great man.” The expression goes back to Plato, who uses it in the opening chapter of his work on the state.

amor mortis Scaeva — Scaeva fought with fierce determination in the Roman civil war against Pompey’s overwhelmingly superior forces. He claimed for himself a “love of death.” See Pharsalia VI, 245–246.
Jus se defendendi contra hostem deponere nemo potest — “No one can give up the right to defend himself against an enemy.” Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, chapter 14.

obéissance préalable — “Prior obedience,” a concept Schmitt took from Maurice Hauriou. See M. Hauriou, Principes de droit public. A l’usage des étudiants en licence et en doctorat ès-sciences politiques, 2nd ed., Paris 1916, p. 804. Schmitt’s copy, with notes and an introduction, is preserved among his papers, RW 265 no. 27583.

Schmitt seems to have first quoted the expression in 1935: C. Schmitt, Was bedeutet der Streit um den Rechtsstaat? in SGN, p. 126. The idea itself, however, had already appeared in LuL as one of the three “premiums attached to legal possession of power.”
Hohe Molmert — A hill near Plettenberg which Schmitt often climbed.
“Toward the Godhead one composes letters that have remained unspoken from the beginning …” — From Theodor Däubler, Attische Sonette (“Der Zug”).
“the piano playing beneath me” — Schmitt’s younger sister Anna Schmitt was a piano teacher and taught lessons in the house they shared at Brockhauser Weg 10.
Bentham’s “Expectation” — Jeremy Bentham, Principles of the Civil Code, 1838.
Coups d’état intellectuels — Paul Valéry, Oeuvres, vol. 1, Paris 1957, p. 815.
Carpe diem; veniet hora — “Enjoy the day; the hour [of death] will come.”
Parmenides, Nebel — Gerhard Nebel, “Das Sein des Parmenides,” in Der Bund, 1947, pp. 87–119.
Prayer of Duns Scotus — See Tb 1930–34, p. 375.
Histoire des Treize — Stories from Balzac’s La Comédie humaine cycle. German title: Geschichte der Dreizehn, published in numerous editions.
Goethe’s idea of the “smallest company” — From Goethe’s poem “Vermächtnis”:

And if at last you have succeeded, And if your whole being has come to feel That only what bears fruit is true, You test the universal course of things; It will proceed according to its way— Join yourself to the smallest company.
Hitler: “My life is a novel” — A remark by Hitler recorded by Hans Frank. See Gespräch, p. 189, note 45.
Eduard Rosenbaum claimed … — No source has been identified.
“The path that led us — Lassalle” — A quotation from the “German Workers’ Marseillaise,” the song of the General German Workers’ Association. It ends with the lines:
“Now we follow the daring path That Lassalle led us along.”

Tantulus homo, tantus peccator — “Such a little man, such a great sinner.” See Friedrich Reck-Malleczewen, Bockelson. Geschichte eines Massenwahns, Berlin 1937. Schmitt owned a marked-up copy of this first edition, which was banned immediately after publication.
abyssus vocat abyssum — Vulgate, Psalm 42:8. Luther: “One depth calls to another.”
“The ocean is free, and freer still are springs” — See above, note to p. 18.
“What Bruno Bauer calls Judaization” — Bruno Bauer speaks of the “Judaization of peoples.” See B. Bauer, Das Judenthum in der Fremde, Berlin 1863, p. 48.
